title: How Does BUBBLE WRAP Protect Parcels? In 1957, It Was Meant for Walls
description:
Bubble wrap was first meant for walls. How did it end up in shipping boxes? Following three US patents granted later, with filing dates in 1957, 1959 and 1960 respectively, this episode separates the jobs of wall patterns, cushioning material and continuous manufacturing. The greenhouse and IBM 1401 packaging connections come from Sealed Air's later accounts; IBM's own history page does not independently confirm the packaging supplier. Illustrations are narrative depictions, not reconstructions of the people, equipment or transactions of the time.

chapters.c04r-e01: Two Films Fused at the Seams
chapters.c04r-t01: Hot Film Sets on the Roller
chapters.c04r-n01: Changing When the Air Goes In

c04rh011.text: Could what you ship face every bump in transit with just two thin films protecting it?

c04rh021.text: Picture yourself at a packing table, pinching a clear, bubbled sheet; each cell holds nothing but air.

c04rh031.text: What interests me most is that these little air cells first appeared in a wall-covering design.

c04rh041.text: Its maker, Sealed Air, later included this beginning in its company history.

c04rh051.text: But the thin seam between the two films would bring an unexpected challenge.

c04rh061.text: Today, follow bubble wrap from an idea for walls to the problems you face when shipping a parcel.

c04rh071.text: It seems to do no more than trap air. How does it take on the job of protecting goods?

c04ro011.text: The wall design called for light, soft, raised patterns; the granted patent sealed air between a film and a backing.

c04ro021.text: That patent, later granted in 1962, lists only one engineer as its inventor.

c04ro031.text: The drawings show wall and furniture coverings, with air cells supporting the surface texture.

c04ro041.text: Thick plastic was then needed to support raised patterns; this design aimed to cut weight with film and backing.

c04roa1.text: In your hand, you want this film to feel light; on a wall, you want the bumps not to collapse right away.

c04ro051.text: Once the film was embossed, where could the backing be glued without flattening every bump?

c04ro061.text: The granted text describes heating a continuous feed of film, then guiding it to a roller with recesses.

c04ro071.text: Vacuum inside the roller pulls the soft film into those recesses, forming raised cells.

c04ro081.text: With the film still on the roller, the glue roller touches only the flat valleys, not bumps tucked into recesses.

c04ro091.text: A thicker, less air-permeable backing is pressed on, sealing each space beneath a bump into an air cell.

c04rob1.text: I find it interesting that air first became a shaping tool. But would people really want that pattern on their walls?

c04ro111.text: The granted text also says the air-cell surface could give furniture a soft feel.

c04ro121.text: The covering could be rolled for shipping. But with backing, could it still bend around curved furniture?

c04ro131.text: The thicker backing supports the film, and air supports the bumps from inside; the thin, light surface can still bend with walls or furniture.

c04ro141.text: Years later, the maker recalled that the two engineers' decorating idea never caught on.

c04ro151.text: The wall idea failed, but the patent left options: plastic or treated-paper backing, with adjustable thickness and stiffness.

c04ro161.text: This flexible, air-filled film left room to turn to other uses.

c04ro171.text: If walls offered no place for it, where else needed a light, thin material with air cells?

c04ri011.text: The company's 2013 account puts greenhouses next: after walls went nowhere, they tried the air-cell film as insulation.

c04ri021.text: The company says this had some marketing success; in greenhouses, the film's air served as insulation.

c04ri031.text: This history comes from the company's account. But how did an insulation idea reach fragile goods?

c04ri041.text: The company's account then turns to one engineer: he saw that fragile goods needed cushioning in transit.

c04ri051.text: The company says he compared air-cell film with paper and old newspapers around fragile goods, and saw trapped air could improve cushioning.

c04ria1.text: If you were shipping something fragile, good looks alone probably would not reassure you enough to seal the box.

c04ri061.text: Walls barely move; shipping boxes are lifted, set down and stacked. When a box wall is hit, what must the film take the force for?

c04ri071.text: The packaging patent names shock absorption during packing as an aim; the cells now had a specific job beyond walls.

c04ri081.text: When the box is hit, the cells and film sidewalls compress first, leaving space to absorb impact between item and box.

c04rib1.text: I think this is where the little bubbles faced a truly tough test: every move could make the goods press them again.

c04ri091.text: But if the two films separated in transit, how long could that row of bubbles protect anything?

c04ri101.text: Each cell therefore needs its own seal; even if one is squeezed, the others must keep their own air.

c04ri121.text: The company says the two engineers kept refining how to make the film after seeing its packaging potential.

c04ri131.text: Making it posed another problem: just-sealed films could lose their raised shape after leaving the hot equipment.

c04ri141.text: The vacuum roller had worked to form the cells, and their air was sealed in. Why could cooling still flatten them?

c04re011.text: The answer is expansion and contraction: as the cell's gas cools, pressure falls, so outside air may flatten the bump.

c04re021.text: The patent proposes sealing at higher pressure; back at normal pressure, the cooled cells can stay inflated.

c04re031.text: Another proposal reheats the flattened cells, shrinking them into smaller but still air-filled shapes.

c04rea1.text: Imagine inflating a little bag: as it cools, the pressure balance inside and out changes. Sealing it is not the end.

c04re041.text: The early wall patent glued backing to the flat valleys; in packaging, that seam had to withstand squeezing.

c04re051.text: Could they join it without waiting for glue to dry?

c04re061.text: The new patent says glue takes time to dry and may make the film bond less even and reliable.

c04re071.text: It heats the films' contact faces, then presses them while the surfaces can fuse, joining them directly into a seam.

c04re081.text: Heat seals a ring around each bump, keeping air in separate cells without relying on glue.

c04reb1.text: When I first read these two designs, it was that narrow edge that caught my eye:

c04reb2.text: the bubbles' job had changed, so their edges had to change too.

c04re091.text: But heat sealing brings a conflict: flat joining faces must stay hot, while the bumps must not melt. How can both be managed?

c04re101.text: Bumps kept too hot lose their shape; the seam must fuse while the formed cells keep their shape.

c04re111.text: The patent keeps contact faces hot and cools the raised parts first; no glue drying means less waiting in continuous bonding.

c04re121.text: But when an impact nearly flattens a cell, what besides the trapped air can offer the goods more protection?

c04re131.text: The patent uses hexagonal cells to show air compressing first; sloped sidewalls add resistance as the cell is pushed down.

c04re141.text: Even if a cell is crushed, the inventor says its sidewalls may keep supporting it before total collapse.

c04re151.text: This is the granted patent's technical claim; not every bubble has this shape. The film itself also cushions.

c04rec1.text: For your shipment, when bubbles flatten, the film must help as well as the air.

c04re161.text: A wall pattern began bearing loads for goods; but had the company formed when this change entered a patent?

c04re171.text: These details appear in a text filed in 1959 and granted in 1964.

c04re181.text: No. The packaging patent's filing date predates the company; filing does not mean the material was sold that year.

c04re191.text: With a packaging use, heating, embossing and sealing still had to work together on a continuously moving film.

c04re201.text: The material keeps moving, but each cell must be sealed. How can the machine bring two films together on time?

c04rt011.text: It sends the films along separate rows of heating rollers, meeting while the air cells are still supported;

c04rt012.text: this is the equipment design in another granted patent.

c04rt021.text: The company formed in 1960. Drawings in a patent filed that March and granted later

c04rt022.text: linked heating, embossing and cooling into one continuous path.

c04rt031.text: This time, two engineers are listed as inventors; the aim is stable shapes as the film keeps moving.

c04rta1.text: Beside a continuous film-feed machine, you can think of it as a relay:

c04rta2.text: material handed on by one stage cannot wait for the next to get ready slowly.

c04rt041.text: Looking at the two roller rows, you may ask: how can film hot enough to wrinkle enter the recesses neatly?

c04rt051.text: The hotter the film, the harder it is to feed it flat into the embossing roller; wrinkles prevent neat shaping in the recesses.

c04rt061.text: The drawings use a spreading roller: as film moves, interleaved surface parts move sideways to flatten it.

c04rt071.text: Parts retract as they turn away from the film, then spread on contact again; the roller repeats this without stopping the material.

c04rt081.text: Vacuum holds the bumps in the recesses, and the second film is pressed on; but if both hot films leave the roller immediately, what happens to the seam?

c04rt091.text: Figure 2 also proposes spraying water after bonding, cooling both films quickly on the roller without separating them.

c04rt101.text: A trough below collects coolant, air dries the surface, and only then is the sheet removed; it can keep moving throughout.

c04rtb1.text: I find this the most interesting part: it looks like simply making film,

c04rtb2.text: but the drawings keep deciding when it must be soft and when it must set.

c04rt111.text: The granted text says the finished sheet can be rolled up. What goods did the company later use to show its move into boxes?

c04rt121.text: Years later, the company recalled bubble cushioning protecting IBM 1401 computers in shipment soon after its founding.

c04rt131.text: The computer maker confirms shipments began that year; the packaging link comes only from the cushioning company's account.

c04rtc1.text: For you, this example makes the bubble sheet's job very specific:

c04rtc2.text: the box must keep traveling, so something has to protect what is inside.

c04rt141.text: On walls, the bumps were a pattern to be seen; inside boxes, they hide and help goods survive handling.

c04rt151.text: Shipping means surviving more than one hit. As the box keeps moving, will its cells stay inflated to the next stop?

c04rt161.text: As air slowly escapes, bumps flatten; the distance they can compress through on the next impact also shrinks.

c04rt171.text: Years later, the maker was still discussing how to stop air escaping. That engineering problem had not gone away.

c04rt181.text: The early packaging patent drew another defense, around the whole sheet rather than an individual cell's seam.

c04rn011.text: A barrier layer wraps the whole bubble sheet; Figure 20 of that packaging patent places it around the sheet.

c04rn021.text: In the drawing, the outer layer sandwiches the film and seals at every edge, adding another air barrier beyond the separate cells.

c04rn031.text: The maker's 2013 account also says they developed barrier protection to reduce air leaking from cells.

c04rn041.text: This is an idea in a drawing; the drawing itself gives no date for its first commercial use.

c04rn051.text: The 2017 brochure still claims longer air retention. But why does another product start out uninflated in the warehouse?

c04rn061.text: Because pre-inflated bubbles already take up space during shipping and storage.

c04rn071.text: At what stage should it be inflated to avoid filling the warehouse and still keep up with packing?

c04rn081.text: The 2017 brochure's product is shipped and stored flat, then inflated at the packing station.

c04rn091.text: This is another product from years later; we cannot project it into the factory in the company's early years.

c04rna1.text: If you run the packing station, you get more than a roll: an inflation step must also keep pace with shipping.

c04rn101.text: The trade-off is compatible inflation equipment at the station; a flat roll cannot be unrolled straight into a box like inflated cushioning.

c04rn111.text: The maker says it saves storage space. But how can a packer take just what this box needs from a long inflated roll?

c04rn121.text: The brochure's cushion has perforations every 12 inches; once inflated, a section can be torn off along them.

c04rn131.text: Once inflated, it still travels through many handoffs with the goods; the maker positions it for cushioning heavier loads.

c04rn141.text: After unpacking, the brochure says it can be deflated and flattened; when to add and release air is now part of the process.

c04rnb1.text: I like this little turn: by the time we reach this point,

c04rnb2.text: even where the air should appear, and when it should leave, have become part of the product.

c04rn151.text: Remember the opening wall? The pattern changed jobs: cells take pressure, while seams and processes keep air there for the goods.

c04rn161.text: In your most memorable unboxing, which item were you most afraid might break? Tell me in the comments.

c04rn171.text: To keep seeing how everyday objects change jobs, and the design choices behind them, subscribe to this channel.
